utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, are you ready for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. [Interpretation] I have the same request as for the previous witness, face distortion and a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I guess there is no objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Usher, could we have the witness, please? Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, my apology. I asked if I could see the Chamber just for a moment before we have the witness just on some procedural matters if I could ask if we could go to closed session or private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My first question: In the police station, is there a detention unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is a.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness come closer to the microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there are two detention units in the Siroki Brijeg police station. That's correct. In the Siroki Brijeg police station, there are two detention rooms, which, during the communist -- which were made, which were owned during the communist regime, because under the then prevailing law on the criminal procedure of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the police had the right to, without the consent of the investigating judge, to detain people up to three days. Those persons for which there were indications that they had committed a certain crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. After the three days, under the then prevailing law you would either release them or bring them before an investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the three days, if we collected enough evidence to file criminal charges, then we, together with this criminal report actually, we would take the suspect to the prosecutor general, to the public prosecutor. And if we did not collect enough evidence during these three days to file a criminal report, then that person would be released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people -- this questions may not be as relevant. Another question about the detention only and the investigating judge could have made decisions about detention; is that right, after the three days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After these three days, only the investigating judge could do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to more specific questions. I am going to be asking you only about one very specific event. In 1993, were a number of Muslims brought to the police station? Was there a large number of Muslims brought to the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In May, 1993, I can't give you the exact date, but I think it was around the 10th of May, when ten members of the Army of BH were brought from Mostar to the police station Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me who brought them, how, and how many people were there, and were you present when they were brought in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day, as on every other day, I was present in my workplace in the Siroki Brijeg police station. These people of Muslim nationality were brought by the military police in two of their vans. Since I was there when they were brought in, I could see that some ten people were -- from one van were first taken to the building of the military police, which is in the same street, in the immediate vicinity of the civilian police, i.e. the Siroki Brijeg police station. In that building, the military police had two improvised detention rooms. And then from the second van, they brought out the ten people who could not be accommodated in the detention rooms of the military police, so they were placed in the two detention rooms of the Siroki Brijeg police station that I've already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the civilian police -- did the civilian police have any jurisdiction over military -- the military that year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The military police had jurisdiction over conscripts and all the military. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then why did they bring to you? Why were those ten people put at your -- put up at your place in the civilian police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because in Siroki Brijeg, these two buildings, that is the military police building and the civilian police building, because thee two buildings were the only ones where there were any strong rooms, any detention rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were you asked to look after them? Because you said that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, allow me to explain it to you in a couple of sentences. When the military police came, and told the chief of the police administration -- no, sorry, police station, now it is called police administration and I sometimes confuse those two terms. They told him that they'd need to put these persons in the detention facilities for only a couple of days, but that they would be only to be guarded by the civilian police so that in the meantime, they could conduct investigation in relation to those detainees as they were suspected of having committed war crimes. On the same occasion, representatives of the military police notified the chief of the police station that during those couple of days, which is how long they ought to be kept there under custody, they would be coming --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Military police representatives. To conduct interviews with the detainees in order to collect evidence about the perpetrated war crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Then who was responsible for those persons in the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for the interviews and all the rest regarding those detainees, the responsibility rested with the military police. The civilian police was only to keep them under custody, because that was what was explicitly said by the representatives of the military police during their meeting with the chief of our police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who could talk with or gain access to individuals who were in your detention unit? And how was this custody organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, those were the people from the military police because they were the only ones responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody else could gain access to them because after those persons were detained, the chief of the police station held a briefing with his assistants, and ordered to inform, to notify, their subordinates that nobody aside from the military police was allowed to communicate with the detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, how many detainees were in each of the detention rooms, in the strong rooms? How were they accommodated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In each one of the two rooms, there were four detainees. And in front of these strong rooms, there is a rather large hall, and on the floor there were sponge mattresses and that is where the others slept, the difference, those who were not in those cells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it with my own eyes, because across the hall from those strong rooms, or rather at the entrance, down the staircase, to the right of those detention rooms, was the laboratory of the criminal investigation department, and sometimes it was necessary for me, because of certain crimes, to go down there to consult the laboratory technicians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was responsible for the custody? Who guarded those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the uniformed police who were responsible to keep an eye on the detainees. Their job description, or rather the rules prescribed that they submit reports every morning to their chief, and he would then submit it to the chief of the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the food? How did you feed them? Tell me all that you know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was wartime and there were very few of us policemen in the Siroki Brijeg police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean professional, law enforcement officers like you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, professionals. We therefore spent all our time on the premises of the Siroki Brijeg police station so that most of the time we even slept there, because we had our cots, our beds, on the upper floor where the police had their premises, that is both the uniformed and the criminal investigation officers. We were getting food from a factory in Siroki Brijeg because it had a very large kitchen and which prepared food for the troops, and from there it was taken out into the field, and within the framework of that, they also brought food to us, to the Siroki Brijeg police station. And that is where we had our meals throughout. The same food which we were getting from this kitchen, from this canteen, from this ready-to-serve food factory, the same food was also served to the detainees. In other words, the food which was getting to the Siroki Brijeg police station was served, three meals a day, and with this food, we were also getting fruit, juices. The food that we were getting, and then distributing among the detainees, this was done -- the distribution was done by their guards, or as I already said, the uniformed police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you perhaps speed up? Now you're just too slow, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those same officers were responsible for --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please speed up because it is important when this dot stops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm watching when the dot stops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The most important thing is that the two of us do not speak at the same time because then the interpreters cannot follow. And speed, try to adjust it. I think the interpreters will warn you if we are too fast and we always have to remember Her Honour Judge Diarra because she's following the French translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So those same officers, that is the uniformed police, who were -- who guarded the prisoners were also responsible for -- also took prisoners to the toilets when necessary, and I mean when necessary, when they asked to be taken there, because that was the orders that they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let us finish with this canteen. Was it a central canteen, a kitchen which prepared food for the troops, or I may not lead you. Tell us, who did this food factory supply with food, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apart from this central kitchen, which was in Siroki Brijeg, there was yet another kitchen in the Obnova company. And it also prepared food for the troops, and that food was taken to the troops on the ground, and a large number of refugees who were in Siroki Brijeg at the time were also getting that food, and also incapacitated people or weak people whose members of the family, whose sons were on the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on, I think we shall come to that. A few words about the refugees. We will come to that. Let us not discuss it now. Tell me now, the Siroki Brijeg police station, who was above it? Who issues orders to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was only and exclusively the Ministry of the Interior of Herceg-Bosna with the seat in Mostar, and the police station accounted to the MUP in Mostar, and received orders from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will later on become more specific but say who would be called to account in if somebody hit a detainee, who would be called to account?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There would be a whole chain of responsibility to begin with, the perpetrator of the act, then the chief of the police administration, because he would have to report to the central ministry of the interior in Mostar, to the central MUP in Mostar, and they could also sanction individual acts. They had this authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had that happened, would you feel moral responsibility for that too because you were one of the chiefs there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, also in terms of my age and my seniority, yes, I was a senior, I was one of the senior people there, if not the oldest person there. So of course I'd feel responsible, because I was there. I participated in those. However, I can say speaking in my own name --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment. Now we shall move to some specific matters. Namely, we heard witnesses testify in this Court how they were beaten in front of the police station, how they were put ten men to a cell in the police station, they never mentioned the military police, they never said that there was such a building as the military police, so only the Siroki Brijeg police station, a that they were ten to a room. And that on various occasions I will give you names later, but we shall go into private session, that they were mistreated and in horrific ways.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Counsel, sir, I'm surprised. I'm really taken aback. How could the Court accept somebody who insinuates things like that? Because all I can call this is shameless lies. I say that there were no such things, that nobody could enter the Siroki Brijeg police station, apart from the military police, because any entrance into the Siroki Brijeg police station had to be recorded by the duty officer at the police station in Siroki Brijeg who had his logbook, and the name of every visitor had to be entered there and the reason for his visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these logbooks still with the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, sure, 100 per cent. They can still be seen, if need be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hope I'll be there in no time at all, and I'll ask for that and I hope you'll help me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apart from the duty officer who would be substituting for the chief of the police station in his absence, the state operations officer will also -- at the Siroki Brijeg police station, and unlike the duty officer of the police station, that person was there to receive telephone calls or was there to hear comments or perhaps information about acts committed and the operations, duty operations officer also assigned officers, policemen, to different jobs, whether they were traffic wardens or the uniformed police, it was his job to give them assignments and to maintain the radio link, to report about the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was not really following because I was looking at the transcript, because I do not quite understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Wait. We haven't finished the interpretation. Yes, please, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Excuse me, it appears page 16, starting on line 15, it's the witness's answer but it shows it in the record as being a question. I know my lead counsel sometimes asks some lengthy questions but the record should reflect that this is this witness's answer starting on line 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think both the counsel and the witness should be as concise as possible. That is the questions should be short, the answers should be concise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know an individual called Ernest Takac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I've never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Romeo Blazevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never heard of Romeo Blazevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel and witness please break between question and answer to avoid any confusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know somebody called Ivan Hrkac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Siroki Brijeg there are several people called that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I tell you that he is the brother of the late Mr. Mario Hrkac, is that the important that you say you know?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not in 1993. Later on, 1997, 1998. Because Mr. Hrkac was with the police administration in Hvar, that is with the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia, in 1992, because before that, he went to the police academy in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say Hvar, us mean the island of Hvar in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long was he a policeman in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he completed the police academy, he got a job with the police administration on the island of Hvar in the county of Dalmatia. And I know that until the beginning of 1994, he worked for that police administration, as a law enforcement officer or rather a uniformed policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this gentleman have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, sure, "Zdral" and he earned that nickname when he was still a boy. Because he's a man who loved animals and he was very fond of birds, and he grew birds at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was called "Zdral"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is the crane, and cranes when they migrate and they reach those areas at a certain period of time, near Siroki Brijeg, there are two large fields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no. We don't have to go into that. Simply his nickname was Zdral and he was named after a crane, after the bird which is crane. I hope the interpreters will be able to interpret that. And who was called Cikota?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His brother, late Mario Hrkac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we heard testimony here that the three of those we've just mentioned, ruthlessly mistreated in your detention rooms the detained persons of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a lie. It simply could not happen, because I say that I spent most days and most nights in the Siroki Brijeg police station, because we took shifts sleeping, so there were always several people on duty there. And since I know Mr. Hrkac personally, I affirm that he did not enter the Siroki Brijeg police station at the time and it is ludicrous to say that, because at that time he was working for the police administration on the island of Hvar so how could he be at the same time in the Siroki Brijeg police station? We are a serious institution, I mean that is the police. And such an institution could not allow anyone access to the police premises to somebody who would go in and then mistreat somebody there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, -- no, my first question. Do you know Mr. Mladen Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Mr. Mladen Naletilic even though he does not know me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean you know who he is but you never met him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never met him, but we all know Mr. Mladen Naletilic, and I used to see him around in Siroki Brijeg, but also before the war, long before the war, I heard about Mr. Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he enter the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Impossible, because he had no business there. I told you that the police is exclusively responsible for the police station and it is under its exclusive jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, could he order them to get there, to be brought there and be kept there, those detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He couldn't. How could he order? He did not have any kind of jurisdiction over the civilian police. It was only the military police who could do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Mladen Naletilic interview them in the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ridiculous. If he didn't enter the police station, then he didn't interview them. And he couldn't enter, because otherwise, his name would have been entered in the logbook, as I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know what the Convicts Battalion is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Convicts Battalion had jurisdiction over that police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's again incomprehensible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe to you but we have to explain all that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I say that the only jurisdiction over the civilian police belonged to the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Mostar, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if the Convicts Battalion had its own detention unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I already said that the only detention strong rooms were in the civilian police and in the military police in Siroki Brijeg, that's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask Madam Registrar to give us D1/342, and then the exhibit, the Prosecution Exhibit 26.9? [In English] Put it on the ELMO, please. Maybe the last picture is the best, the last one, yeah, the last one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [interpretation] Can you tell the Honourable Court what is in the photo? Can you sharpen it a little? Can you focus it a little? You can look at the one in front of you. You don't have to look at the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I take it in my hands? This is the military police building, and before the war, it was the committee building which is in the vicinity of the civilian police, and this is where the strong rooms of the military police were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What committee? You mentioned a committee.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the party committee of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now the second exhibit, 26.9? Can you please take the pointer in your hand? It works like an antenna. You can extend it. First, are you familiar with the photo? Do you know what it represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is the tobacco station in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please show me the buildings -- the buildings in which the army was, the buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no troops there, just the command, commands of certain units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show me where the commands were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me which commands, which army was in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The command of -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the witness is too far from the microphone. The interpreter didn't catch that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the Home Guard units, the civilian protection of the Siroki Brijeg Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: He pointed at a house and I'm not really sure whether the transcript it was correctly reflected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik would you please have the witness mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours, because of you, Your Honours, I wanted to resolve the enigma of the tobacco station, so we will discuss every one of these buildings because the witness lives there and is familiar with the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please encircle the building which housed the commands and mark it with number 1, but not on the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can he put it on this exhibit? Maybe -- no, this picture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [witness marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, can you repeat, who was in this building, all the institution that is were in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The building housed the command of the Siroki Brijeg Brigade -- the Siroki Brijeg Brigade, the command of the Poskok Battalion, the command of the Home Guard Battalion, the command of the Convicts Battalion, civilian protection, and the ambulance unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this house also house a detention room or a strong room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was no strong room in this building. The only strong rooms in Siroki Brijeg were in the buildings of the military police and the civilian police. These buildings do not have underground rooms. None of these buildings here have basements or underground rooms. These -- these buildings, are for that matter devastated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please take the pointer in your hands and can you please point to the buildings which you said were devastated, that do not serve that purpose, and if they don't, since when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This building, the entire complex here, the buildings on the flank, the buildings in the courtyard inside, the only building that serves its purpose is this one on the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a pencil -- the pencil in your hand and mark the buildings which do not serve their purpose which are not being used and mark them by numbers, 1, 2, 3, 4 and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, there is a word that's been translated as devastated a couple of times and in the sense in which it's been used, it cannot be correct, that there were no cells in the buildings because the buildings had been devastated, devastated is destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Croatian when something is run down, we will say devastated. When something has been abandoned and in a very bad state of repairs, then we will use the word "devastated" but not destroyed, not in the sense that you understand it. So run down, abandoned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask what the witness now is describing, in what time period are we talking now? Is this all 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: All time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'd like to be clear, also on the month. Because if he says that this house commanded, which period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you may ask this question to your witness instead of answering it by yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not answered. I have allowed my witness to answer all my questions, and I have instructed my witness that all the time we will be talking about 1993, and as for the buildings, the first logical question would be since when have these buildings been abandoned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you'll allow me, I would like to say a few sentences about what the tobacco station is, what did it serve, what purpose it served before the war and what purpose it has served after the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But before that, can you encircle the building which still serves its purpose, which is still in function? You did say that one of them still -- is still being used. Which one is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the tobacco station was built, I don't know when exactly, but I believe that it was before World War II. Since in Siroki Brijeg there was practically no industry, quite a number of people went abroad to work there as temporary workers, but people in the villages and in the suburbs of Siroki Brijeg mostly lived from agriculture, given the climate at the agriculture crops which were grown, the only thing that could grow there was tobacco. The tobacco which used to be sold in the tobacco station. This is where the tobacco was traded. Even before the war, the tobacco growers were not paid enough by the tobacco station, so they lost economic motives to engage in the tobacco growing. And that's why nobody was any longer growing tobacco. So that's why nobody was selling it to this tobacco station. A few years before the war, these buildings were abandoned so there was nothing there, and in time, they became run down and obsolete. And these buildings were where tobacco was fermented and dried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you please show us the buildings you're talking about and also show us with the pointer which buildings do not have a basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- there is nothing to show because none of these buildings have a basement, a cellar. And all these buildings served for the fermentation, i.e. drying of tobacco. But I don't know where the -- where tobacco was packed and repacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that the building was devastated, i.e. run down, you meant that it did not have any windows or doors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are stone buildings which were built a long time ago. What I meant was the rooms. These rooms have wooden floors and -- and I don't know why, whether it was because of the technology of tobacco drying, whether that is the way it was built at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the windows and doors, do they exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were broken long time ago. People -- children from the surrounding villages would come here in the evening and play in these buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it's the time for a break, and I would like to inform you that I will finish 15 minutes after the end of the break. I have a few more specific questions, and I will end with those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just finish with the tobacco station. The building that is still used or was still used, what was it? What was in the building, in the command? No, the other building that you put a circle around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under number 9?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, take the pointer and point to the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean this building?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the Defence department. It was here even before the war, but before the war it was called the Secretariat for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it that a part of the municipality of Siroki Brijeg? Was that a municipal secretariat or a municipal department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here on the right-hand side in the green, greenery here, can you tell us, is this a swimming pool?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, you can't see it very well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the city -- the town swimming pool.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show it to us and can you tell us -- was it used and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The swimming pool was built a long time ago and I used to swim in there when I was young, but then it wasn't used for a while, until some two years ago. Then it was re-- renovated and now it is again being used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark the swimming pool by number 10?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise, I had a brief consultation in order to make this examination as efficient as possible. My first question now is about the detainees which were in your building, in the police station. Were they taken to the forced labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not taken to the forced labour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, do you personally know, what was going on in the building of the military police? Did these detainees go to work, to forced labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what went on but I know that they were not taken to the forced labour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, were you at the police station when the military police organs were interviewing these detainees? That's the first question. But let -- first ask me whether they were interviewed in your building or were they taken to their building for interviews?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were interviewed in our building on the first floor of the building of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the interview, were the detainees treated correctly? Were you in the room when they were being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were there tending to our every day duties and we would go from one room to another. We would spend sometime in our office and then we I would see them when they were being taken for interviews, I would see them in the corridors and then when they were taken back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they ill-treated or was the behaviour correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not ill-treated. If they had, I would have known that. My colleagues would have known that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned refugees. Let's maybe finish with that. What did you mean when you mentioned refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately before the Serbian aggression on Mostar, a number of refugees, some several thousand of them, came to the area of Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were their nationality, their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Muslims and Croats. They were accommodated in the areas of Kozice and Medjine. These are two villages with Muslim population. Then in Siroki Brijeg, in the pupil's home, in the church, and in the elementary school in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that? What year were they there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992, after the aggression against Mostar, and in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout the entire 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that they were there until either August or September, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they receive the food from this kitchen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from these two kitchens, from the factory and from the -- Obnova company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It has just occurred to me to ask you my last question along these lines. We were talking here about the name, Siroki Brijeg. Since when has Siroki Brijeg been called Siroki Brijeg? Has it ever changed its name throughout history, and why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Siroki Brijeg has always been called Siroki Brijeg, until 195 -- I think 1952, when the then communist government changed its name to Listica. Listica is the river that flows through the centre of Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions for you. Thank you very much for coming here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any -- no? Yes, Mr. Bos, for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Bos:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness, my name is Roland Bos and I will ask you some questions this afternoon on behalf of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let's discuss the prisoners who arrived on the 10th of May. You stated that on the 10th of May, a group of Muslim prisoners arrived in Siroki Brijeg and that the military police came to the civilian -- to the MUP station and asked that some of these Muslim prisoners could be taken in your office; is that correct? In the cell of your office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any prior notice that these prisoners -- that these POWs, the POWs would be arriving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was any prior notice. I know that on their arrival, they actually contacted the chief of the police administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who contacted the chief of the police administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A representative of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that contact, there was a request to take some of these prisoners in the MUP station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. We were briefed, which was subsequently conveyed by the chief of the police administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any objection by the chief of the police to take these prisoners? Because I would assume it's not a really normal situation that a civilian police would take prisoners of war in their cells.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether in their conversation any objections were raised. However, under the law, the military police has the right to bring in certain persons if there are indications that they had perpetrated a crime. I've already said that given the fact that these were the only detention facilities in Siroki Brijeg, that that is why these detainees were put there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you say that under the law they had a right to detain prisoners, I would assume that it's to detain prisoners at their own facilities, not at facilities of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was only talking about detention, which is allowed under the law. About keeping somebody in custody. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if I say that during a wartime situation, if a military police is requesting the civilian police to take prisoners in their detention cells, is that something that would normally be accepted, given the wartime situation? So in other words, would the military police have authority over the civilian police in that sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military police did not have any jurisdiction over the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on the 10th of May these prisoners arrived without any hesitations, these people were detained at the civilian police, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've already said that a representative of the military police talked with the chief of the police administration. And the chief of the police administration is duty-bound to notify his ministry, and he said that he had obtained the consent of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the police station in Siroki Brijeg? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Danko Bilinovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he also have a nickname by the name of "Cane," C-A-N-E?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cane, sorry. That was his nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 26.4, 26.7 and 26.8, please? First 26.4. Witness, do you recognise what's reflected on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the building of the Siroki Brijeg police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you now also could look at -- I think they are in front of you -- Exhibits 26.7 and 26.8, do you recognise what's reflected on those photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. These are the detention rooms in the Siroki Brijeg police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that in both these cells, there were four prisoners, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I say that that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of any of the prisoners that were kept at the MUP station? And if you know any names, maybe we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we don't need to go into private session. Now, Witness, I'd like to make a few things clear. First of all, how long did these prisoners stay at the MUP station? Do you know that? Let's say that they arrived on the 10th of May. How long did they stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly, eight to ten days. Not more than ten days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And according to your testimony, they did not leave the MUP station during that period? They -- during that period, they remained within the MUP station all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not how I put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they actually sometimes leave the MUP station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After a few days, after they had been brought from Mostar and detained there, the military police came and now I don't know exactly but I believe they took away three or four detainees so that six or seven men remained under detention. And they came out, I have already said that, they came out of the detention rooms, because -- to go to the toilet. And the lavatory and shower booths which were used by the civilian police when they changed shifts, that is when they would come back, so they also used those facilities when they needed them, that is to relieve themselves or to have a shower.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood the question you say that they left the cells but did they also leave the building when they were detained. Did the military police ever take them out of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military police would come from time to time and take away two to three men, and then bring them back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they would be taken away in the morning and then come back in the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. It would be -- they would be absent for a few hours. According to the military police, they took them to military investigating authority, that is what they would tell us when they took the detainees out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during those ten days, the eight to ten days that these prisoners were kept at the MUP station, how many of those days were you actually at the MUP station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that of those eight or ten days, while I cannot be quite -- cannot say quite exactly, but perhaps I was not in the building one day, maybe two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all these other days, you were there during the day and during the night as well, as you testified, that you would actually sleep there as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's true. I mean yes, by day and by night, I would come out into the passage with the uniformed police because we were very few in number, so that -- so that very few people went out on patrol so there was always somebody in the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask how many police officers would normally work in this -- in this office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you clarify, please, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you had the uniformed police and then -- well, you had the commander and I don't know whether there were any other functions but the total group of persons working in that building, how many people were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact number, but the criminal investigation branch, service, there were five of us. And the uniformed force, I believe ten, maybe 15 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was the uniformed force who were actually guarding the prisoners, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that these prisoners were interviewed by the military police in the MUP station. How often were these prisoners interviewed? Was it on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not on a daily basis. At times, two days in a row, and then there would be a break, and then it would start again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they always interviewed during the day or also sometimes during the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Always -- no, mostly by day but I would allow also that they came at night too. I think as far as I can remember, that they came one night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they would interview these witnesses at night, from what time to what time would this interview be conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I said I remembered that they only one night came, it means that there were no more interviews by night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, during that particular night, from what time to what time was the interview conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it could have been between 8.00 and half past 9.00, not after 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that the interview would have stopped before 10.00?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know where these prisoners were taken after they were taken out of the MUP station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, can you clarify what you mean? Do you mean the -- those early days when three or four were taken away or when they were finally taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. When they were finally taken away. Do you know where they were taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the military investigating prison in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this period, was this the only time that prisoners were kept at the MUP station, or were there other occasions where prisoners of war were kept at the MUP station, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the only time, I know that definitely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So none of these prisoners who were kept at the MUP station at that time, you ever saw coming back again at the MUP station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified that you knew Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, and that he was a well known person in Siroki Brijeg, that everybody in Siroki Brijeg knew him. How come that everybody in Siroki Brijeg knew Mr. Tuta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tuta came to the area of Siroki Brijeg, or rather I saw him in early 1992 for the first time, but a number of people knew about him even before the war, because he had donated various things to Siroki Brijeg. I know personally, at the time when I was an active athlete that he used to send donations, that is he used to send sports gear to clubs in Siroki Brijeg, except for the youngest members.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, interpreters' correction especially for the youngest members of those clubs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that he provided funds for the St. Anthony's chapel at the entrance to Siroki Brijeg, and since in Siroki Brijeg, or rather in all those, in this whole area, people are very religious, large numbers of people attended evening services in front of this chapel because St. Anthony is particularly appreciated, held in -- particularly revered in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you say that he sent donations, from where did he send these donations? Where was he when he sent these donations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think Germany, I think, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's talk about Tuta now in 1992 and 1993, during the war. What was Tuta's role in this war, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what his role in the war was. All I know is that he is one of the founder of the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you saw him -- you never spoke with him but you saw him sometimes in Siroki Brijeg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him, did he ever wear a military uniform or a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw Mr. Naletilic in a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in the direct examination, you were asked about this man Ivan Hrkac, and you seemed to know him pretty well. And apparently, his brother is Mario Hrkac; is that correct? And his nickname is Cikota, no?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you repeat the answer? The interpreters didn't catch the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't answered yet. I haven't answered. You were asking me about Mario Hrkac, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters are asking you to repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have to repeat my question and you have to repeat the answer for the interpreters. Now, is it correct that Mr. Mario Hrkac's nickname was Cikota?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. The late Mario Hrkac was nicknamed Cikota.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know -- you mentioned him as the late Mario Hrkac. Did you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know he was killed sometime around the 20th of April, 1993, in the area of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend his funeral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You have to come a bit closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Tuta was also present at that funeral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P36.1, please? You can put that on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise any of these people who are depicted on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me who you recognise and could you point them to -- with the pointer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is General Praljak. Mr. Vice Vukojevic. General Ivan Andabak. Mr. Mladen Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is Mr. Mladen Naletilic wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the photograph is not particularly clear, but it could be an army uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's move on to the tobacco station, and maybe we can put Exhibit 26.9, which was already marked by the witness, on the overhead projector. Now, Witness, you seem to have quite some knowledge about this tobacco station. How often would you visit this complex? And I'm talking now specifically about the period 1993. Did you ever visit at the complex in that year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's be more specific. Let's say from the period May, 1993, to December 1993, so more the second half of 1993, how often would you visit this complex?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. Could have been a few times. I cannot give you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the reasons for you to visit that complex?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I knew Mr. Marinko Mikulic, who was the head of the Defence Department, and I knew Mr. Vlado Maric, too. He was the commander of the Poskok Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which particular building would you then visit if you would be there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in this building once, and this one here, I visited that one once or twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that building which you first indicated, you've stated that also the Convicts Battalion had their headquarters there. Who do you know from the Convicts Battalion was in that office, or you don't know, or do you not know any names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Mr. Ivan Andabak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whom do you mean? Will you please explain? Who do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did any other people from the Convicts Battalion held office there of which you know the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have that knowledge, no. Only Ivan Andabak had the office there, otherwise, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've stated that the Home Guard Battalion also had an office there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I cannot really know about the terminology -- I'm not sure about the terminology. Volunteer, either volunteers or the Home Guards. I think Home Guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the role of the Home Guards? What was their function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, their function was to guard their houses in their neighbourhoods, they didn't go to front lines outside their neighbourhoods. They places, they were there to guard their homes, their homesteads, their neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Home Guards have any role in guarding prisoners in Siroki Brijeg, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I do not know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they would only guard the homes, and they had nothing to do with guarding the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not had too many interventions because this cross-examination has been very connected. I just wanted to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. say that the witness has misunderstood the question. I'm listening to the Croatian interpretation. The way the witness interpreted was what was the general role of the Home Guards. And I believe that my learned friend wanted to find out about the role of the Home Guard in Siroki Brijeg. So can you repeat the question and explain whether you -- what you had in mind was just Siroki Brijeg and the Home Guard of Siroki Brijeg or generally speaking the Home Guard units?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, the witness testified in chief that the Home Guard was situated in the tobacco station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which Home Guard was situated in the tobacco station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say that it was any particular Home Guard Battalion. I said that it was just their command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The command of what unit? I mean we are not talking -- was that the command of the specific unit of the Siroki Brijeg Home Guard or the command of the general Home Guard which was in the tobacco station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear that the Home Guard had any special units at all. I'm talking generally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the question, I think, should have been put which command of which brigade was in that particular building, and it would be clear. I believe that the witness doesn't actually understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bos, if you believe that is important, you may ask some specific questions on this very issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, I do believe it's important. All right. We will have to be a bit more specific, then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Witness, let's go step by step. You've stated in your testimony in chief that there was a Home Guard Brigade stationed at the tobacco station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the Siroki Brijeg Brigade, which originated from these battalions, the Poskok Battalion and the other three I mentioned. I meant the Siroki Brijeg Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's the Siroki Brijeg Home Brigade and it's your testimony that the Siroki Brijeg Home Brigade had nothing to do with prisoners but they would only guard the homes in Siroki Brijeg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But of course. I'm only -- I can only refer to the period of the month of May. You have already asked me about that, and I don't know which detainees are you referring to. I don't know of any other detainees ever being detained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of this Home Guard Brigade was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now that I understand your question, I've -- all the time I'm talking about the Siroki Brijeg Brigade, and I think it was Mr. Cavar, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does the name Jablanica mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. It's a little town on the road from Sarajevo to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the village Jablanica but about a person named Jablanica. Maybe I spelled it wrong, or maybe it's a nickname.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't know any such person. I don't know a person under that name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's briefly look back at the photograph. That will be my final questions. Witness, under -- under number 8, the building marked under number 8 do you know what was -- who was stationed in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever visit that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I know where the building is. I would go to the Defence Department but I did not enter this building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never entered this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Briefly. Re-examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the cross-examination, the Prosecutor asked you whether there were any other detainees, military personnel, were they ever detained in the civilian police. If there were any detainees that belonged to the army, who may have committed some crimes, where would they be taken to? Where were they interviewed? If it was a military person, regardless of whether it was the BH Army or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only in the detention cells of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My second question: Can you tell the Honourable Court the person whom you know under the name Vice Vukojevic whom you recognise. Do you know what is his -- what he is today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that he is one of the judges of the constitutional court of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another question about the funeral: How many people attended Mr. Mario Hrkac's funeral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several thousand people. That was absolutely the biggest funeral in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally see Mr. Naletilic or did you hear that he was there, or did you see him personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would be all. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Questions from Judges? Judge Clark? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Witness, can I ask you about the duties of the civil police at the MUP station? Is it your evidence that when these detainees arrived, whatever their status, that the civilian police had some role in relation to their welfare?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only role they had was to guard them and that was it, to assist them with their every day needs. That was food, hygiene, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, if we ignore for a moment the detainees that came to the station on the 10th of May, you described how there would be a duty officer at the station. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was a duty officer which also was there in the peace time. Every police station has a duty officer who receives reports, either over the telephone or if people came to the station in person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Was it the function of this duty officer to record in the logbook any visitors who came to visit a detainee, a prisoner, somebody in custody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already said that the duty of the officer, of the duty officer, was to record anybody's entry into the police station and the reason for their being there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: On this particular eight or ten days that you described to us, would the duty officer have kept a record every time one of the detainees was removed for interrogation or every time a military policeman came to interrogate him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Every such event was recorded in the logbook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, in a police station in my country, the duty officer has a function to ensure that the person whose liberty is being taken away, the person who arrives under arrest at the police station, is informed of certain rights. I'm not saying that that happened during the war. But the duty officer has to record the person's name, his date of birth, his height, and his condition. Is that the situation or was that the situation in your police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already said that the exclusive jurisdiction over these detainees belonged to the military police. And that the duty officer was -- it was his duty to record people entering the police station, every time somebody entered the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, would he have entered the name of a military policeman who came for the purpose of interviewing a certain detainee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So can we take it that the name of the interrogating officer and the name of the person being interrogated would have been recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Are the logbooks annual log books or do you start an anyone as soon as the last page is completed in the existing logbook?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you complete the last page, you open a new logbook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And what happens to the completed log books?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is then archived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you know who is in charge or who was in charge of the archives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The chief of the police administration had the exclusive jurisdiction and the person in charge of the archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You suggested to Mr. Krsnik when you were giving your evidence that these documents can be produced. So obviously you know how to gain access to these a -- archives. It can't be very difficult?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not difficult. You can gain access to them at any given moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I hope the Defence and the Prosecution are listening. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Diarra?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Witness, I would like to ask you the following thing. You knew about the presence of Mr. Naletilic at the beginning of 1992. According to your own words, he was a well-known, because of the donations that he gave to the population and even the church there. In addition to that, did he engage in other activities? Did he have any other, to your knowledge, things that he engaged in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he didn't engage in anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have said that he was one of the founders of the Convicts Battalion. At the level of that battalion, what was his role, according to what you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, in that battalion, he was only looking after his men, after his families, the families of the soldiers who were at the time on the first front lines, the families which had been left behind on their own, and the families of the fallen soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't have any other activity in the command, in the coordination? He only looked after the families of the soldiers? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, that was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judges' questions? Yes, Mr. Krsnik? Further examination by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one. To follow up on Her Honour Judge Diarra.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in 1992, in the -- what was going on in Siroki Brijeg in 1991, 1992, the Serbian aggression, did Mr. Naletilic play a role at that time, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He may have played a role of a coordinator during the Serbian aggression, but if you're implying to a command role or participation in that, I think it's ridiculous, it would be ridiculous to expect of somebody of his age to ramble around the hills and command any military operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to hear from you personally what you knew, not what you heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that he ever took part in any command operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the direct command operations on the first front line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the Serbian aggression, what was the situation like in Siroki Brijeg? How far did the Serbian forces -- how close they came to Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in the surrounding hills, some half an hour from Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. I just wanted to ask my witness whether he is aware of any activity in Siroki Brijeg with regard to Mr. Naletilic. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Boss?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour. Further cross-examination by Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness you just answered in response to my learned colleague, let me just look at the transcript, that he may have played a coordinating role in the Serbian aggression. What do you mean by coordinating role or coordinator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have then misunderstood me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm just reading the transcript. That's what it said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I meant is that he, as one of the founders, that he maybe wanted to know what was going on, what was happening to his men, the men that he looked after. That's what I meant. That he wanted to be informed about any operations that ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from answering the questions of Judge Clark, is it your testimony that in Siroki Brijeg, the controlling and care of prisoners and detained persons, that was all very clearly regulated and that procedures were strictly followed and that there was nothing vague or non-clear about the control of the prisoners and who was responsible for that? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I repeat that. I've already said it. Everything was correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were talking about the archives. Where are these archives where these logbooks are kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left and joined the police in Mostar. I believe that it must be either in the police administration in Siroki Brijeg or the relevant MUP of the Western Herzegovina county in--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last word? Could you repeat that last sentence because the interpreter didn't catch the last word, the county in?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the seat of that county, the name of the seat of that county.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the MUP of the relevant county, so it can be either in Siroki Brijeg or in the seat of the Western Herzegovina county.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor asked to you repeat the name of the town in the Western Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Ljubuski. That is the seat of the Western Herzegovina county.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Witness. Thank you for your -- to come here to give your evidence. When the usher pulls the blinds down, he will show you out of the room. We all wish you good luck in your future.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and I wish you the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I would like to just tender Exhibit D1/342, the exhibit that has three photographs. I also formerly P26.9 as marked by Witness NG will have a new number. D1/43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No objections from the Prosecution side, and we don't have any exhibits to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So those two documents are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, are you ready for your next witness? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I must be ready and I'm always ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, are there any protect -- protective measures for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
