utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am very tired. Can I ask for a break? And then if we can proceed with the witness, and the protective measures that I'm asking for are face distortion and a pseudonym, if that may be granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I believe there is no objections from the side of the Prosecution so your request for protective measures is granted. And we will take an early break and we will resume at 20 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we go into private session for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, are you going to ask for closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It is just one matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe I could ask you to take the floor first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm only doing this because I know at 7.00, everyone is anxious to leave and I don't want to hold anyone up. Yesterday, Mr. President, Your Honours, the Chamber requested, invited submissions in connection with the structure and workings of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Prosecution has filed today and provided copies to the Defence and I provided a binder for each of you, Your Honours, it looks like this, submitting materials on Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Dayton Peace Plan, and the structure of the current state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much but I did not expect that -- it's a bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, when you invite it, we give it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we go to the private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, the technical booth, could we have the ELMO down, please? Examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, to begin with, good afternoon, Witness. I have already informed Their Honours about the complaints that you are suffering from, and if you have any problems, please let us know and we shall make a break. Are you all right now? Are you feeling all right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First I must ask you, look at the monitor in front of you, and this is what I'm saying to every witness, you see that black dot which is moving, so look at it. When it stops, then you can start speaking. The most important is that we do not speak over one another, because then the interpreters cannot follow. So find some average speed because if you're too fast, the interpreters will warn you. So try to -- not to go too slow but still, don't be too fast either. Now you will be shown a sheet of paper with your name there but do not utter your name aloud, just tell us if that is in your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now go into private session, the private session means nobody else can hear you but those present in the courtroom. That is what the private session is. Nobody else will know what we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in those hard times, which struck the area that I lived in, that my co-nationals lived, we had to do something in order to be able to function. Grave things happened. A war happened, an unwanted war, a war which brought -- which affected all peoples in a horrible way. The war started, suffering started, a large number of refugees came to Siroki Brijeg, panic spread, and one needed to somehow calm the situation down, do something so that people could start functioning again. My friends, people of prestige in the municipality of Siroki Brijeg, together with politicians who were in Siroki Brijeg at that time, and I talked about what we could do, because we are all responsible for that state of affairs, and we simply had to do something. And it befell -- it came to my lot, even though it could have been any other of those men whom I see on this list, and who are my closest associates, but, well, simply, [redacted] [redacted] So it was a voluntary office and I managed to persuade, and they were also ready to help the town, various gentlemen including the gentleman who is present here in the dock, Mr. Mladen Naletilic, and my friends, Mr. Ante Banozic and -- for Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. -- Other gentlemen, and a professional team headed by Mr. Zdravko Kutle who was responsibility for economic affairs, Mrs. Zdravka Bevanda, who was responsible for general affairs. Mr. Mario Kraljevic for financial affairs. Mr. Danko Bilinovac, who held an office in the Ministry of the Interior, Mr. Marinko Mikulic, the Defence department, and the only party man that was representative of the HDZ was Mr. Zdenko Cosic, these four persons, the first four, were all volunteers and those others were professionals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of all those people, only one was politically active. None of the others were members of any political party, is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Not one of them, except the last one, Zdenko Cosic, not one of those others were members of any political party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Naletilic held what office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Mr. Naletilic, in view of his experience from the war in Croatia, that is the war against the Serbs, was responsible for the logistics and provided the link with the units which were in the area of Siroki Brijeg at the time. As a war veteran he helped us a great deal to organise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please be so kind and tell us briefly, you said that the situation was chaotic, but briefly, because I'd like us to finish today, if possible, perhaps you could tell the Court what was so chaotic in Siroki Brijeg? And how did you then organise the civilian life? What was your principal concern?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Well, naturally, after the military operations, everywhere in the world, and that includes our area, a large number of refugees whom we accommodated in our area, in the area of Siroki Brijeg, so that our sports halls, our schools, our families, took in those wretched people who had to be fed, who had to be provided with a roof over their heads and as you know, in a house, there is always a person and we have to bear this in -- who is somebody who is responsible for that family. [redacted], it was my job to see to it that they did not go hungry, that they were protected, and to do that, I invited those men to help me, and there was -- they were all powerful men. Mr. Mladen Naletilic, a well known man who did his utmost, who did a great deal to protect those people. Mr. Banozic, Mr. Hrkac, that is all those people here helped in one way or the other, and those companies in Herzegovina did not work, with the exception of those which were outside, and those were the only ones who could set aside some aid, and provide for those people. At our first session that we held, we also appealed for help to our people in the diaspora, and addressed all those who could help us and especially those unfortunate people, those refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the next question is what ethnicity was that of the refugees and how did you protects them, how many of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: We simply never divided the refugees according to their ethnicity, a refugee is a refugee is a refugee, never mind what ethnic group they belonged to so we had Serbs and we had those of Bosniaks and naturally there were very many Croat refugees who had fled from other areas, and come to us, because in Siroki Brijeg, there were no military operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Did you organise soup kitchens or something else? How did you feed those people? What go the humanitarian relief? How did you make do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: The humanitarian relief, we were fortunate in Siroki Brijeg to have in the commissary in Siroki Brijeg and we have a fryer there, Jozo Zovko [phoen], who was also well known, not only in Siroki Brijeg but around the world who had many connections could therefore organise the relief. We also had many people in diaspora abroad who were also helping us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you about that because I have a document that will be my next question, but I was just asking you about those kitchens?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, yes, we had it organised at the municipal level, that is we had two points which provided food, not only for the refugees but also for other people who needed such relief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were those kitchens?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: We had two kitchens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for whom did they prepare food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: One was at the Feral and the other one was at the Obnova company and they provided food both for our troops and for the refugees and for people who could not look after themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I will show you D1/345 and after you've seen that exhibit, I will ask you to explain to the Court what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have D1/345, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: We took a decision that our migrant workers abroad, rather than come back to defend their hearth, we bound them to somehow financially help, and we decided that every citizen who was -- who worked abroad was bound to pay 300 marks to the account of the municipal of Siroki Brijeg every month. And that accounted for 90 per cent of our budget of the revenue that we had in Siroki Brijeg. The rest of the money, we raised, we introduced -- we rather levied a war tax on the companies that were still working, and we did get some small funds from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whom did you then finance from the municipal budget?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: This municipal budget was used to finance, and the most important thing was to finance our families or rather the families of our defenders. We had to see that the -- our defenders' family would be looked after, that they don't go hungry and from that money, we also in a way also financed our volunteer Siroki Brijeg brigade. And the other units who were in the territory of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, could you just tell us which were they, which were the ones that you financed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: From the republic -- from the municipal budget we financed our volunteer Siroki Brijeg brigade which incorporated one special purpose unit, the Convicts Battalion, which was a part of that brigade, and which Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was responsible for special interventions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So somebody else could ask for its help? It wasn't exclusively and only attached to that brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: No, it was not exclusively attached to that brigade. It could also be assigned to other areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. But it had -- it used the logistics of that brigade. Could you please explain what was the link between the two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: The Convicts Battalion originated in 1992 during the war against the Serbs, and it is called the Convicts Battalion because it brought together men who were -- who had persecuted, punished, incarcerated, that is simply people, the accused gentleman here, Mr. Mladen Naletilic, came at that time to Siroki Brijeg, I mean 1991, 1992, he came bringing with him his experience and, well, let's put it that way, his knowledge, and he managed somehow in those hard times, when everybody had taken to his heels, when everybody was hiding in whatever holes, they managed to somehow motivate those people and embark on the defence of these territories against the Serb units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say punished, why were those people punished?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Well, if we go back a little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But just briefly, will you explain the Court, if you know, that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, there was major persecution of those people from our territories who had to emigrate, and one of them is the present Mr. Mladen Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Because he was at odds with the then regime. Most people were at odds, disagreed with that regime, but some people did not flee abroad and lived as they did always longing for their -- and those who were abroad always yearned, always longed or always felt home sick.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why, and so the name came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: And they were called the Convicts Battalion because they had suffered punishment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean for political reasons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: For political reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us now cover only the period when you took up the office that you did, and 1993, moving into 1993, I will ask you specific questions and please give me specific answers to them. Now, do you know where the personnel of the international community in Siroki Brijeg was accommodated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Yes. I know it well. I know well where the seat of the international community there was because it was customary, as soon as the HVO was founded in Novi -- in Siroki Brijeg, the international community was invited, and informed about people who had been appointed to the HVO. There were several, now perhaps I won't be able to remember the names of all the people from the international community, well naturally, I will recall the names who --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, let's then move on. Did you ever meet Sir Martin Garrod?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Sir Martin Garrod is my friend and I spent a lot of time with him in Siroki Brijeg. They came very often, well, naturally, on official business, to the municipal council, but also very often, almost every day, they were my guests at my place, at my property, and Sir Martin was -- we all liked him. He particularly struck the eye or rather the ear because he every day learned a new Croat word. His pronunciation was as it was but we all liked it very much. Besides, besides, frequently when we met, naturally, he liked to say, well, "to have a glass too many," and then it was very nice to talk with him, to socialise with him, and other people came with him. I remember there was a Spaniard whose name was Jesus and so on and so forth. Sir Martin Garrod at that time was Jesus's assistant, Mr. Jesus came from Spain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Garrod told us here that there were very interesting people who lived in Siroki Brijeg, and that they were extremists.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: That is very strange if Sir Martin said that. He never said that while he was there. At least he never said it to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever meet with Mr. Naletilic in your house? Let me give you the date. 15 August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: As far as I know, I never saw Sir Martin Garrod with Mr. Mladen Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you talk to him or how did he talk to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: They always had interpreters with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where Ivic Pasalic was born, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Honourable Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: He was born in Suica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir Martin Garrod told us that he was from Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Mr. Ivic Pasalic is from Suica. That is a place between Livno and Tomislavgrad, some 80 kilometres away from Siroki Brijeg, if not more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your conversations with Sir Garrod in your place, were they official or private?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Our official conversations took place in my office in the HVO office in Siroki Brijeg, and when he visited me in my place, those conversations were private. And that's why I am very surprised that my good friend, Sir Martin Garrod, could abuse the private conversations in which we could talk privately about anything. And these conversations are usually not binding on anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move to another specific subject, that is Mr. Mladen Naletilic. My first concrete question: Was Mr. Mladen Naletilic in 1993, was he a soldier or did he have a rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Mr. Mladen Naletilic was not a soldier, and he did not have any ranks. He was in charge of the things that I mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your personal knowledge, did anybody at the time have a military rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody had a military rank. There were just responsibilities as per individual functions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, did he participate in the conflict with Muslims? Again I am referring to the period of 1993, that is the subject of this examination.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: I claim that Mr. Naletilic did not participate in the conflict against Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, since you've mentioned the Convicts Battalion, who was its commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: As far as I know, and as far as I could read in documents, that was Mr. Ivan Andabak, at my time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Mladen Naletilic ever the commander of the Convicts Battalion, to your knowledge, personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Mr. Mladen Naletilic is one of the founders of the Convicts Battalion, and as far as I know, he was never its commander. But he did help with the organisation of the Convicts Battalion. The commander of the Convicts Battalion, as far as I know, was the late Mario Hrkac, Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: I'm referring to the period of the fights against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you -- do you mean operations commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Yes, operations commander. Mr. Mladen Naletilic was not up to climbing any mountains, as you can see, or leading those people up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he took over this office that is mentioned in the document, was he in Siroki Brijeg all the time? And what were his main duties, concerns?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Mr. Mladen Naletilic was with us very often, as often as was needed, in order for us to discuss and arrive at decisions as to what needs to be done. His concerns matched his experience, and his duty was to help these people in coping and to help these people to be supplied, to have everything that was needed by a soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any special duty with regard to the implementation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreter did not understand -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was funerals, did he have any duty with regard to funerals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: These were the most difficult moments, the funerals of our soldiers, and Mr. Mladen Naletilic had the courage, had the strength, to talk to these people, to convey his condolences and to be -- to help them at the most difficult moments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he do that officially on behalf of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Yes. He attended every funeral on behalf of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he wear a uniform, a military uniform? Did you ever see him wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Only on special occasions, and funerals, these funerals, were one such special occasion. It was customary to wear a uniform. We all wore uniforms for such occasions, even us in the civilian authorities, we would wear military uniforms, because these were special moments, the most difficult moments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the construction of the house on Cigansko Brdo, very often in these discussions this house is referred to as Mladen Naletilic's villa.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Counsel, I do have knowledge about the construction of that house that you refer to as villa. No, it is not me. Others do. I claim before this Court, maybe this Court will have the opportunity to visit that area and see for yourself that at least 50 per cent of the houses there are much bigger and much more beautiful than Mr. Naletilic's villa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was the contractor who performed the construction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: I happen to know that. I know who the constructer was, it was a company which engages in the construction, and which still exists and is active in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know whether detainees worked on the house or around the house of Mr. Mladen Naletilic, those inmates were allegedly Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to that until some foundation is laid for this witness's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What foundation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you may ask some questions around the house, whether the witness was there at this period, whether he has passed through those areas during that time. Then come to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours. I just wanted to be as short as possible and I just wanted to reduce my examination to one question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let me rephrase. Do you have any personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been to the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the construction and after?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Yes, during the construction and after, and before the construction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I now ask the witness whether alleged inmates worked on the house or around the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Counsel, I think that a question put in that way to any of us in our area would -- it would be a disgrace to have people who are not paid and who are not -- whose job it is not to do that, that people like that were to work on a house. So I claim before this Court that no -- no other than the competent company and its people worked on Mr. Mladen Naletilic's house. I don't know any of these people but I know the owner of that company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there ever a water supply system built on Cigansko Brdo? Is it possible to build a water supply system there? [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Counsel, it is possible to build a water supply system there. However, even today, as we speak, the town of Siroki Brijeg, the Listica locality, over 60 per cent of households there still don't have water from the main supply. In order to bring water to Cigansko Brdo, to the place where Mr. Naletilic's house is, according to the estimates of some experts, we would have to spend a minimum of 5 million dollars. These are the figures which cannot be borne, even the most expensive places, let alone Siroki Brijeg municipality, and there has never been any word about the construction of the water supply system on Cigansko Brdo, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now let's move on to our last topic. Do you have any personal knowledge that there were Muslim detainees in Siroki Brijeg in July -- June, July and August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Yes, I do know, because [redacted] [redacted], I had to look after about -- I had to look after everybody, because I was responsible for everybody who was in Siroki Brijeg at the time. I know the office that was in charge of that, the Defence Department, came by the information that the military police had brought these people for some interrogation, for some interviews, and that these people were to be placed in some appropriate accommodation. My office, the Defence Department, did manage to find some rooms, very -- in the same building where the Defence Department was. There were some 20 beds there. And these unfortunate people, I referred to all these people as unfortunate people regardless of whether they are Croats, Serbs or Bosniaks, for the mere fact that something like that befell them, so all these unfortunate people have to be protected and have to be treated with dignity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who was looking after these people? Where were they accommodated? Can you explain the location? Where were they accommodated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: That was in the town, in Listica, in the area of Listica, where once upon a time there was a -- the tobacco station. There were some buildings there that had been neglected and run down. Some of -- one of those buildings was refurbished and in that building there was the Defence Department, and next to the Defence Department, there were these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you Exhibit 26.9. Can you please take the pointer and point this building to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: [Indicates] This building behind the Obnova, which looks incomplete. I can see just the roof on the Obnova, and that's this building behind this with the white roof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show us which buildings were not in use and which ones were in use?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: I have to look more carefully. All these big buildings, this one and then these buildings behind, they were in a very run -- in a run-down state. And the only building which was used at the time was this house, this building here. And this building housed the 1st, the 2nd, and the 3rd Battalions, the civilian protection office and this is where the Convicts Battalion also had its headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last questions and then I'll give you over to the Prosecution, were these detainees taken to forced labour? Do you have any personal knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Counsel, never, [redacted], nobody was forced to work. I was in consultation with Mr. Martin Garrod, I asked him what we could do for these people, making sure that we would not jeopardise their human rights, I asked him how we could help these people to engage, to help them pass their time in a better way. Mr. Garrod said that it would be good that -- to give these people something to do, to help them in that way, to -- in order to make their days go quickly. They were probably there waiting to be exchanged. I don't know why they were there. I don't know that. I don't know why they were there. This was not my area of competence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did they actually work? And if they did, did they engage in voluntary work or did they have to? Were they forced to work? What did Mr. Garrod tell you, since you've mentioned him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Mr. Garrod said that these people could not be forced, should not be forced, but if they -- these people wanted to work, that they could. An opportunity was given to us, given the fact that the life was not functioning in Siroki Brijeg as in peace time, we had to build a transmitter on a hill top some 200 ways [as interpreted] from the centre of the city and that's why we had to dig a 200 long -- 200 metre long trench, in order to lay the cables for this transmission pylon. So there was a company engaged this that work, it was a professional company, and the detainees were the ones who were there to help and for that they were given cigarettes, they had bigger rations of food, and they were paid 5 German marks per person a day at the time in Siroki Brijeg that was a lot of money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were paid from the municipal budget?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Yes, they were paid from the municipal budget.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question: You said you knew Mladen Naletilic. Can you describe him as a person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: I know Mr. Mladen Naletilic. We are friends. We are childhood friends. Mr. Mladen Naletilic, it is very difficult for me to find the words at this moment to describe the nobility, the soul of the person who had empathy for the suffering people, for children, the person who helped the entire region while he was abroad, as the person who was persecuted and had to go abroad to work there. I know that he did a lot for the region. He sent donations for sports organisations. He built the St. Anthony's chapel. On this very day, there are mothers praying in that chapel for their children who perished in the last war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Defence, the Defence has no further questions. Thank you very much, sir, for taking the trouble to come here. I know about all your complaints, and that is why I would like to specially thank you for coming here to give your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, are you feeling tired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You still have 20 minutes to go. Are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Any questions from Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric? Cross-examination? Cross-examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher's assistance, if you could move that one panel back just a bit? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just to be -- just as we get started to clarify something, there is another [redacted] in Bosnia-Herzegovina that during the time around 1993 or 1994, was elected or became at least the vice-president --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. We cannot say the witness's name in an open session. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I move it be redacted, Your Honour. It was my mistake and I ask that it be redacted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember how you reacted when I made a similar mistake? How you personally reacted?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness NH, it's my apology to you it was a mistake on my part. It will be redacted and it will not be broadcast out of this room. Again my apology. If we could go to private session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I merely wanted to ask you to ask the Prosecutor, he has given us no documents for the cross-examination of this witness, does it mean that there are no such documents? We wouldn't want to be given this these documents tomorrow because I'm entitled to see those documents before the cross-examination begins. Does it mean that there are no documents, that no documents will be used?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think Mr. Meek has used the phrase, Catch-22, because at this moment, the Prosecutor is in this kind of situation, the Catch-22 situation, that he really doesn't know whether to provide you the documents before or withdraw it until he's using it at a later stage. Let us hear what the Prosecution will tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, you're absolutely right. You're forecast our position exactly, although having said that, I am prepared to give these -- there are only four exhibits and I'm prepared to give them to Mr. Krsnik, although frankly in light of our conference yesterday, I did consider doing it differently, but I'll be happy to provide them to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the rules keep changing we just, as Defence counsel would like to know then because we believe the rules were that documents would be provided before cross-examination began. Now, cross-examination began 20 minutes ago. And it's nice that they are providing them now but we don't understand why. A clarification of the rules would be nice. One additional matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes, we will stick to our rules that those documents should be provided to the other party at least before the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, it is very late but I wish to draw your attention to one matter. Today, from our learned friends received, as you did, some -- accompanying the explanation of constitutional law matters and having to do with the structure of the BH government, but I just cast a look, I just cursory looked at them and these documents include some expert opinions, the opinions of expert groups. I think that this is the Prosecutor's attempt to bring in something through the back door, something completely different, something that has nothing to do with the concept of the BH government. I do not know whether it is a new proposal of the Prosecution how we should treat it, if it is nothing new, then could they were draw that part of the documentation which we received earlier in the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for drawing our attention to this very point. We haven't received those documents yet. We don't know what is in it. In my view, those documents were not tendered for the evidence into this case. It's just to help us to understand the meaning of the BiH government. If you insist, we will ask the views from the Prosecution whether they would like to withdraw it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. However, the Defence believes that you do not need such an unilateral and biased view that was put down on the paper by some crisis group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, I believe when we asked the parties to help the Chamber, those views submitted by the party is one-sided. That's quite clear. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Unilateral but objective. And this has nothing to do with your request. I absolutely second my -- Mr. Seric, and I'm really surprised at myself, what kind of a head do I have? I have to get an examination and then I couldn't go -- I was really flabbergasted when I saw the first document or two. This is not what you asked for and I support Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
